All right. This is divine rule. So we're going to read two books of the Bible: Ezra and Nehemiah. These books are important but not often discussed by scholars. Ezra shows how Persia helped the Jews reconstitute their nation through a process that gives insight into current thinking in Israel, allowing us to analyze future behavior.

In the first year of King Cyrus of Persia, God prompted him to issue an edict declaring the permission for Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. Cyrus did this because God commanded him, not out of imperial ambitions. 

Thus says King Cyrus of Persia: "The Lord, the God of heaven, has given me all the kingdoms of the earth. He has charged me to build his house at Jerusalem in Judah." Permitted Jews could go up to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple with assistance from their communities. Cyrus also financed the rebuilding.

However, when the Jewish exiles returned to rebuild the temple, locals were upset over their presence. This conflict benefited Persia’s divide-and-rule strategy.

When the builders laid the foundation of the temple, priests in their vestments stood ready to praise God with trumpets. Levites, including sons of Asaf, performed rituals as instructed by King David. They sang, praising and giving thanks to the Lord, who is good and whose steadfast love endures forever for Israel.

This moment was the happiest in Jewish history when they rebuilt the temple, now called the Second Temple. The destruction of this temple later led to plans for a Third Temple on the site of Al-Aqsa Mosque, the third holiest site in Islam. Thus, according to the Bible, Israelis aim to destroy Al-Aqsa Mosque to build the Third Temple or Solomon's temple.

Adversaries of Judah and Benjamin approached Zerubabbel and the heads of families when they heard that the returned exiles were building a temple, demanding to participate in the construction.
